translation:
_jahan kabir tahan rarankar. rarankar tahan kabir aadhara ||_
_rarankar kabir hi gaya. tathe ramkabir thaherava ||_
_aur baat suno chit lai. jame sab sandeh mit jai ||_
_radhakrishna vrindavan vasi. puran brahma aadya avinashi ||_ (Where Kabir is, there is Rarankar; where Rarankar is, there Kabir is the very foundation. Kabir himself sang of Rarankar, and so he came to be known as Ramkabir. Listen further, with your mind fixed on this, for it dispels every doubt: Radha-Krishna, dweller of Vrindavan, is the full, primordial, imperishable Parbrahma.)

(Krishnadasji's Parachari)

In setting out the practice of devotion (bhakti), Shyamdasji states that the finest devotion is Kabirji's devotion. Devotion must be pure — and pure toward Parbrahma alone, not toward any other deity or god. This is why Kabirji taught worship of "Rarankar" — Rarankar being the pure, nirgun (without attributes, formless), untainted Parbrahma, whose name is a single-syllable sound. Yet when we speak of this same full Parbrahma in its embodied, sagun (with attributes, embodied) form, it is "Radha-Krishna," the dweller of Vrindavan. Both these forms are, thus, the finest paths for devotion. Devotees, therefore, should worship the flute-charming Morli Manohar Parbrahma without dispute — whether they practice sagun devotion or the formless, single-syllable nirgun devotion of Rarankar — because:

_rarankar bina aur na jaano. devi dev kachhu nahi maano ||_
_ramkabir jehi mukh gaave. aur baatke nikat na jaave ||_ (Know nothing other than Rarankar; give no heed to any goddess or god. Whoever's mouth sings of Ramkabir need go near no other matter.)

In pure, unmixed devotion there is no room whatsoever for maya (illusion) — maya is the great danger on the path of devotion, and worship of gods and goddesses yields nothing but worldly wealth, nothing more. But those who desire devotion alone must give up the worship of gods and goddesses, and should instead take up the repetition and remembrance (jap-smaran) of the single-syllable name "Rarankar," or the five-syllable name "Ramkabir." Let us pause here and speak a little of Onkar. Shyamdasji relates that after taking initiation from Jivanji Maharaj, Krishnadas Maharaj asked him to explain the Original Being (Aadya Purush) to him, since the six schools of philosophy (shad-darshan) all teach the worship of Onkar, yet none of them attain Parbrahma through it — so would Jivanji Maharaj kindly explain this to him? Jivanji Maharaj then said:

_aadya purush vrindavan vasi. aadya purush hai avadh vilasi ||_ (The Original Being dwells in Vrindavan; the Original Being also delights in Avadh.)

— for these two forms are one and the same. Further, at the time of the creation of the universe, Onkar came into being, and it took refuge in maya.

_tabto onkar hi bhayo. mayako sharno teen grahyo ||_ (Then Onkar alone came into being, and took the refuge of Maya.)

Because of this, the creation born of Onkar became bound by maya, and no one came to know of it.

_onkar tab srishti nipaai. taki khabar keenahu nahi paai ||_
_aadya purush te bhoole tabahi. onkarkun laage sabahi ||_ (Then Onkar brought forth creation, and no one came to know of it. From that moment, all forgot the Original Being, and all became attached to Onkar instead.)

Thus, in the creation born of Onkar, everyone forgot Parbrahma and clung to Onkar instead — that is, it was as if they abandoned the root and clutched at the branch. They took Onkar itself to be the full form of light, and declared it to be the full Brahma — and from this arose the twelve names of Brahma. We will not go into the account of the time of creation at length here, since that discussion will come later. But of those who worship Onkar, Shyamdasji says:

_onkarko esa roopa. andh dhandh mayako koopa ||_ (Such is the form of Onkar — the blind, entangling well of Maya.)

This is a well made of maya. Just as a sightless person falls into a well, in the same way, any person who stumbles in choosing a path of worship without any knowledge or thought falls straight into this well of maya that is Onkar's form — and once a soul has fallen into this well, only a capable Guru can rescue it. This is why the path our Guru has laid down for us was set forth only after deep thought and understanding — for even a supreme devotee of Onkar-worship like Krishnadasji himself climbed out of just such a well. By his good fortune he found a Guru like Jivanji Maharaj, and so he attained true devotion; otherwise he would have had to pass again and again through birth and death in this cycle of transmigration.

The importance of this chapter lies precisely in this: which form should one worship? Whom should we hold as our chosen deity (ishta) and worship? Who is our ishta-dev? It is to settle questions such as these that Jivanji Maharaj has held this discussion here. Carrying this discussion further, Kabirji's sakhis (couplets) are now given.

_kabir nirakarke paar hai. parbrahmka noor ||_
_tahan kabira ram raha. jahan sakal brahma bharpoor ||15||_ (Kabir is beyond even the formless — he is the very light of Parbrahma. There Kabir dwells, where the whole of Brahma is fully present.)

_kabir ham vasi undeshke. jahan brahmka koop ||_
_avinashi binase nahi. aave jaay swaroop ||16||_ (Kabir: I am a dweller of that land where lies the well of Brahma. The imperishable never perishes; it is only forms that come and go.)

_kabir ham vasi undeshke. jahan avinashiki aan ||_
_sukh dukh to vyape nahi. sab din ek samaan ||17||_ (Kabir: I dwell in that land where the writ of the imperishable runs; there sorrow and joy hold no sway — every day is alike.)

_kabir ham vasi undeshke. jahan chakvi kare malaar ||_
_nishdin samare saikun. bisre nahi lagaar ||18||_ (Kabir: I dwell in that land where the chakvi bird sings the raga Malhar; day and night it remembers its Lord, never forgetting Him even for a moment.)

_kabir ham vasi undeshke. jahan baare maas bilaas ||_
_brahm (prem) jhare kamal bikase. jahan tej punj prakash ||19||_ (Kabir: I dwell in that land where there is delight in every one of the twelve months; where Brahma — that is, love — streams forth, the lotus blooms, and there is a mass of radiant light.)

_kabir kartam karta na hota. na hota hat aur pat ||_
_tab tha kabira ramjan. jine dekhayo ghat ghat ||20||_ (Kabir: when there was no doer of any deed, when there was neither market nor cloth — that is, before this creation existed — even then Kabir, servant of Ram, already was; it is he who has shown God present in every single heart.)

_kabir paani pavan ambar. na hota na hoye onkar ||_
_tabka das kabir hai. so kaha jaane sansaar ||21||_ (Kabir: when there was no water, no wind, no sky, when even Onkar had not yet come into being — Kabir was God's servant even then; how could this world ever come to know it?)

_kabir adhar jalechu. adhar dhar adhar aas vishwas ||_
_adhar kabira hi mile. adhar nirantar baas ||22||_ (Kabir [dwells] in the unsupported ether [unclear]; in that unsupported state he holds hope and faith. Only in the unsupported is Kabir found; in the unsupported alone is his eternal abode.)

Kabirji is saying that the light of Parbrahma lies beyond even the formless (nirakar) — it is there that Kabir is able to reach. That is, Parbrahma is beyond both the embodied (sakar) and the formless (nirakar). God is not the true focus of this dispute [between the two paths] — that is merely a worldly controversy. Engaging in scriptural debate or conquering all directions [in argument] is not enough to know His true nature, for none of this leads to the vision of Parbrahma. Parbrahma is imperishable; He never undergoes any of the six modifications [of material existence] (birth, growth, transformation, decline, decay, and destruction) — it is [only] forms that come and go, while the Full Form itself is never diminished. He has no doer above Him. He is beyond both joy and sorrow. Thus does Kabirji state the matter about Parbrahma with complete clarity.

Kabirji has also said this, in his book the Bijak:

_sunahu sabne mili bipramatisi. hari bin boodi naav bharisi ||_
_brahman haikai brahm na jaanai. gharmein yagya pratigraha aanai ||1||_
_je sirja tehi nahi pahichanai. karam bharam lai baithi bakhanai ||_
_grahan amavas saayar pooja. swaatike paat parahu jani pooja ||2||_ (Listen, all of you, together — the wits of the Brahmins have failed; without Hari, their boat has sunk and filled with water. Though born as Brahmins, they do not know Brahma, and in their homes only perform sacrificial rites and accept ritual gifts. They do not recognize the One who created them; caught in ritual and delusion, they merely sit and expound upon it — falling instead into [superstitious] worship of eclipses, the new moon, the ocean, and the Swati constellation's raindrop.)

Kabirji is saying: O brothers, listen! The Brahmins (vipra) have no wisdom left; without Hari, their boat has sunk — that is, those Brahmins who remain caught up in ego have had their intellect die within them, and they have drowned in the ocean of worldly existence. Such so-called Brahmins are unable to know Brahma, and instead go on performing sacrificial rituals in their homes. But they neither recognize the Creator, nor cultivate any longing to recognize Him. Instead they merely extol ritual action, and remain absorbed in wrongful worship and observance — such as worship tied to eclipses, the new-moon day, the Swati constellation, and so on. Thus they have turned away from the truth and been drawn toward falsehood instead. He continues further:

_swarath laagi rahe ve aadha. naam let jas pavak hadha ||_
_ramkrishnaki chhodini aasa. padhi gunijo kirtimke daasa ||_ (Those who remain fixed only on self-interest take God's name as though it were mere bones cast into fire; they have abandoned their hope in Ram-Krishna, and instead become servants who recite and praise only worldly fame.)

But the soul that has come into this world and become absorbed only in self-interest — such a person's intellect has been destroyed. That dull-witted soul is incapable of recognizing the truth; he has set out upon the wrong path. He has, further, given up even his faith in Ram-Krishna, for one who seeks only wealth, occult powers, mantras and spells, or worldly pleasure cannot truly worship the pure, supreme reality that is Parbrahma Ram-Krishna. Indeed, this is a very difficult thing, for who can give up wealth, riches, and worldly pleasure and still worship Parbrahma? Only a rare soul like Krishnadasji —

— only some rare, exceptional great soul can turn away even from devotion to his chosen deity Ganpati and turn instead to the path of devotion. Today the whole world is running after material pleasure, and yet the world remains unhappy, for however great one's wealth, it can never grant true happiness. Therefore, one should give up a selfish disposition and come to know the one Parbrahma alone.

Here, to help us recognize the form of Parbrahma, some quotations are given from Govind Das's work, the Sarvangalila.

_sada vasant hot he. aad ant aur aaj ||_
_roop aroope saamlo hari. bhagat sadharan kaaj ||23||_ (It is ever springtime there — in the beginning, at the end, and today as well. Whether in form or formless, the dark-hued Hari acts always for the sake of His devotees.)

Here we see, further clarified, the same thing about the form of Parbrahma and the essence of devotion that we have already seen in the words of Jivanji Maharaj and Kabirji. Spring (vasant), too, is a season full of beauty — yet Kabir and others also speak of a nirgun spring, one that lasts all twelve months of the year. That is, in devotion there is only spring, always spring — never any autumn there. This same Parbrahma, whom Kabirji has sung of, this Morli Manohar Parmeshwar, has been sung of by Jayadevji as well:

_kasturitilakam lalatapatale vakshahsthale kaustubham ||_
_nasagre varamauktikam karatale venuh kare kankanam ||_
_sarvange harichandanam sulalitam kanthe cha muktavali ||_
_gopastriparivestito vijayate gopalachudamanih ||23||_
(Geet Govind – 2-10) (On His forehead is a tilak of musk, on His chest the Kaustubha gem; on the tip of His nose a fine pearl, in His hand a flute, and on His wrist a bracelet. His whole body is anointed with fragrant sandalwood, and around His neck hangs a string of pearls (muktavali). May the crown-jewel of the cowherds, surrounded by the cowherd women, be victorious.)

That is: wherever Shri Hari's leela (that is, His devotion-inspiring play) takes place, there it is ever spring — that place is Shri Vrindavan. At the end of the great cosmic cycle (kalpa), in the time of dissolution (pralaya), the three gunas, the five elements, and the fourteen worlds are all destroyed — yet at that very time, not even a single portion of Vrindavan (the nirgun realm) is ever broken. There it is ever spring; Vrindavan remains ever whole and undivided. Even in the time it takes to close and open one's eyes, not even a quarter part of that leela is ever broken — it remains ever unbroken. Such is the Morli Manohar whom Jayadevji has sung of — that is, Jayadevji has shown just such devotion, and it is this very devotion to which Adhyaruji bears witness (Kadavu 4-1):

_hari hari kahaan shyamalvaran gaiye e. mrigmad tilak vishaal ||_
_baal sundar ati raliyaman e_
_harijine kanak mugatmen shohamano e. bethan re maanek kod ||_
_zabakle heera ravi jesa e_
_harijine kaane kundal kote kanthalo e. ur muktaphal-haar ||_
_haar kaustubh mani zalhale e_
_harijine motidun laheke chhe naashika e. manimay kankan haath ||_
_ratan jadit bhuj berkhan e_
_harjine paheran peet parodi e. ur chandan chaa lep ||_
_todar khoop kusum ghanan e_ (Sing, sing of Hari, the dark-hued one — bearing a broad musk tilak on His forehead, a beautiful, utterly enchanting child. On Hariji's golden crown countless rubies are set, sparkling like diamonds, like the sun. In Hariji's ears are earrings, around His neck a necklace, and on His chest a garland of pearls; His necklace's Kaustubha gem glitters brightly. On Hariji's nose a pearl gleams, on His hands are gem-set bracelets, jewel-studded armlets on His arms. Hariji wears a yellow silken garment, His chest anointed with sandal paste, and His anklets are adorned with many flowers.)

Such praises of Parbrahma did Adhyaruji sing — and it is that very Morli Manohar Parmeshwar who came to Ambarish's aid (to help him); He is indeed the true Lord. A sakhi (couplet):

_amarish gohare aaviyo. sundar shyaam saroop ||_
_so nand dware jivna. je dashrath kul badbhoop ||24||_ (He came at Ambarish's cry for help, in His beautiful, dark form — the very one who dwelt at Nand's door as Krishna, and who as Ram was the great king of Dashrath's lineage.)

That is: this Morli Manohar Parmeshwar came to protect King Ambarish in response to his cry, and the account of this is given here. In ancient times King Ambarish was a true and steadfast, supreme devotee of Krishna, whose devotion was utterly sincere. But there was one obstacle: he kept the vow of Ekadashi. In order to attain heaven, he observed vows and fasts and the like — and so it was as though, on a golden plate, there remained a single iron nail. Because of this he fell into difficulty, and so the Lord had to come. Why did He have to come? Because King Ambarish kept the vow of Ekadashi. The reason for keeping this vow was so that one might go to the heavenly realm and be freed from the torments of the realm of Yama (hell).

Here Jivanji Maharaj explains, describing a beautiful episode: once, the sage Durvasa came to the city of Dharampuri-Sanjam, to the house of Dharamraj Yama. Dharamraj gave the sage a most hospitable welcome and served him with great care. Pleased by Dharamraj's service, the sage said: "O Dharamraj, I am very greatly pleased — ask for whatever boon you desire, and I shall grant it!"

Dharamraj (Yama) said: "O best of sages! If you are truly pleased with me, then show me a kindness and grant me this favor: in the city of Ayodhya there is King Ambarish, of the solar dynasty — I wish for his vow to be broken. For the king, together with all the citizens of his city, keeps the Ekadashi-Dvadashi vow with strict discipline, and because of this, all his subjects attain heaven, and my own path — the path to my realm of Yama — has been closed. So if you would kindly cause this vow to be broken, then souls would come to my realm once again."

Durvasa said: "O Dharamraj, I give you my word — I shall break Ambarish's vow." Having given this promise, Durvasa came to Ayodhya, to King Ambarish.

King Ambarish served the sage most attentively. On one occasion, the day of Ekadashi-Dvadashi arrived, and the king kept the vow. As was his daily custom, Durvasa went out with his disciples to the river to bathe and perform his daily rites. At this the king said: "O best of sages! Your daily rites take you until midday. Today I keep a vow, so please return before the auspicious hour passes, so that both our religious observances may be duly kept."

Durvasa went out from Ambarish's palace to the riverbank with his disciples, to perform his daily rites — but there was deceit in his heart. He had no intention of returning in time for the breaking of Ambarish's vow: if the king ate before he returned, his own honor would be violated, and he could curse him and thus break the vow that way; and if the king waited for him and did not eat, the vow would break of its own accord anyway. Thus he planned to trap the king from both sides at once. Thinking this, Durvasa deliberately delayed his bathing and other rites. Meanwhile the king waited, but Durvasa did not come. He even sent servants to fetch him, but Durvasa still did not come. King Ambarish had prepared the offering and the meal with due reverence, but everyone was at a loss as to how the meal could be taken without the sage. The auspicious hour of Dvadashi was about to pass, when Vasishtha, the family guru of King Ambarish, spoke: "O royal sage! Take a sip of water with a tulsi leaf in it — this will not break your vow, and Durvasa's honor, too, will be preserved, for you may take your full meal after the sage returns."

King Ambarish did exactly this — he sipped water with a tulsi leaf in it. When Durvasa learned that the king had taken this sip of water, he declared that his own honor had been violated, and flew into a towering rage, and began to pour a torrent of curses upon the king. In his fury he cursed the king to take a thousand births and deaths in the mortal world. Then, pulling a single lock from the matted hair on his head, he conjured from it a kritya (a curse-summoned avenging spirit), which advanced to burn the king to ashes — yet not the slightest change of expression crossed Ambarish's face, nor was he in the least afraid. Meanwhile the utterly enraged kritya advanced in fury to strike the king — but the very instant she struck, she herself was consumed by flame and reduced to ashes. For upon hearing the sage's curse, the Lord of the Universe had already come to protect him. How He came — the Puranic verse describing that occasion is:

_agratah shri nrisimhashcha prishthato devakisutah ||_
_ubhayapaarshvatah syatam bhratarau ramalakshmanau ||24||_ (In front is Shri Nrisimha; behind, the son of Devaki; and on both sides stand the two brothers, Ram and Lakshman.)

A similar verse occurs also in the Shukadeva [account] and in the Ramayana:

_agratah prishthataschaiva parshvatah mahabalau ||_
_aakarnapurnadhanvanau rakshetam rama lakshmanau ||8||_ (Meaning: From the front, from behind, and from both sides, [Vishnu protects] — for as long as the whole expanse of the sky-world resounds, Ram and Lakshman, their bows drawn to the ear, stand guard.)

Ambarish, in its spiritual sense, means one whose very "ambar" [sky, expanse] is the Lord [Ish] Himself — one in whose every vein and fiber the Lord dwells; and it is such a king whom the Lord Himself, in person, protects.

God comes in person to protect His devotee. For the protection of King Ambarish, the Lord had already appointed the Sudarshan Chakra, which was ever protecting the king. When the sage's wrath fell upon him, the Lord became alert. The wrath that possessed the sage was itself like a form of death — as if it were an incarnation of great Rudra himself. To protect His devotee from such a wrathful sage, the Lord threw a shield of protection around him on every side: in front, Nrisimha; behind, the flute-bearing, Kaustubha-gem-wearing, yellow-robed Morli Manohar Krishna; and on either side, Ram and Lakshman, bows in hand. No fire or weapon could burn or pierce Ambarish's body — such was the unseen, protective shield that guarded him. When Durvasa hurled his curse, the flames of the kritya turned back upon her, and she herself was burned to ashes. The Lord's Sudarshan Chakra then advanced toward the sage himself — its flames wrapped around Durvasa's own body. Having acted against the Lord's own devotee, Durvasa was forced into disgrace, and his matted hair came loose. The Chakra pursued him from behind, and the sage, crying out in great anguish, fled from that place to save himself.

Fleeing from Ambarish's palace, he went for refuge into the assembly of the gods. The divine assembly took fright, and the gods said to him: "Go to Brahmalok, to Brahma." So he went to Brahmalok — but on looking behind him there too, he saw the Chakra, and grew afraid of being burned to ashes. There Brahma said: "O Durvasa! You have committed an offense against a devotee of Vasudev — so if I were to grant you shelter, I too, together with Brahmalok, would be burned to ashes. You will find no refuge anywhere in the three worlds — so go instead for refuge to the Lord of Vaikunth. Only by taking refuge in Him will you find liberation." Thus, distressed and terrified, Durvasa went to entreat the Lord of Vaikunth; he went and offered full prostration, tears streaming ceaselessly from his eyes. Durvasa writhed like a fish out of water; the wailing sage sang the Lord's praises — for it was he who, in his wrath, had conjured the kritya to kill King Ambarish.

It is worth knowing something about kritya. The scriptures state that such powers (shakti) wear a garland of human bones around their necks, and that their dwelling place is said to be Meru, or the sushumna, that is, the spinal column. There are six practices in tantra-shastra:

1) The removal of afflictions, the uprooting of harmful workings or powers, and the counteraction of the evil gaze of malefic planets — this practice is called Shanti or Pushti-karma; it means the removal of practices harmful to a soul (disease, kritya, planetary affliction). In other words, we may call this the subduing of troubles that are spiritual (adhyatmik, i.e. disease), material (adhibhautik, i.e. kritya), and celestial (adhidaivik, i.e. planetary affliction).

2) Vashya, or the act of attraction — bringing others under one's control.

3) Obstructing another's movement is called stambhan.

4) Sowing discord among one's opposing powers is called vidvesh.

5) Driving [an enemy] out of the land is called uchchatan.

6) The intent to take a life is called maran.

These six practices each have their own presiding deity: Rati, Vani, Rama, Jyeshtha, Durga, and Kali (death). Their worship has five ritual components (panchopachar): sacrificial offering, fire-oblation (hom), repetition of mantra (jap), the offering of the vital breath (pranavayu), and self-surrender. Thus, this Durvasa — whose very name means "one whose desires (vasana) are evil (dur)" — conjured a kritya to kill Ambarish. But Ambarish, in his spiritual sense — one whose "ambar" is the Lord Himself, in whose every vein and fiber the Lord dwells — was a king before whom this vile kritya could accomplish nothing. Because the king had broken his fast merely by sipping water, Durvasa flew into a rage, shook loose his matted hair, and drew from it a burning kritya (a power — Meldi Devi, who is regarded as the clan-goddess of the Bhangi community) and set her upon the king. She rushed at the king with full force, yet the king did not so much as flinch. The Lord, to protect the king, had already set the Sudarshan Chakra upon him — and so the Chakra, itself blazing with fury, ready to consume everything, instead consumed the kritya. Seeing the Chakra, Durvasa fled for his very life.

_gam samaan bhojan nahi, jo koi gamko khaay ||_
_amarishne gam khaiyaan, durvasa tan lhaay ||15||_
_krodh sabanko kaal hai, krodhi hai janjaal ||_
_shiv durvasa krodh bas, bahut bhaye behaal ||16||_ (There is no food equal to [swallowing one's own] distress — blessed is he who can "eat" his distress and endure. Ambarish "ate" his distress in patience, while Durvasa's own body burned instead. Anger is death to all; the wrathful man is himself caught in his own snare. Even the great sage Durvasa, overpowered by his own wrath, was reduced to a most wretched state.)

There is also a further verse, which says:

_tapasvinashchapi munirmahatmanah, sadbhaktavaryeshu prayojito vritha ||_
_yathaabhimanah sahasaiva hanyate, durvasaso draupaditoambarishatah ||9||_ (Even the pride of an ascetic, a great-souled sage, when wrongly turned against the finest of devotees, is instantly destroyed — as happened with Durvasa's pride, through Draupadi and King Ambarish.)

The pride even of an accomplished ascetic and great sage, when directed in vain against the noblest of devotees, is instantly destroyed — just as it happened to the sage Durvasa, through both Draupadi and King Ambarish.

_bhakti drohakara ye cha te seedanti jagatraye ||_
_durvasa dukhamaapannah pura bhaktivinindakah ||10||_ (Those who betray devotion suffer throughout the three worlds. Durvasa, who once scorned devotion, thus fell into such affliction.)

Those who betray devotion suffer in all three worlds; Durvasa, who once disparaged devotion, thus fell into such misfortune and distress.

Kritya: she is called the goddess of the utterance of death — through her, many are destroyed. For causing such a vile act, the Samagam applies to Durvasa the epithet "bhurluccho," meaning "wicked one." This kritya is, in essence, [what results when] worshippers of dark, tamasic powers — spirit-mediums (bhuva), ascetic-impostors (bava), sorcerers, and other such impure devotees who follow the path of charms, threads, tantra and mantra for the sake of their own desires and pleasures — give no thought to right or wrong. Such selfish people do not consider whether harm will come to themselves or to others; hence it is said:

_raja rama yamo vanti par dukh na jananti ||_
_prahune baal yachak ashtamo hem kutaka ||11||_ (A king, a woman, Yama, a spirit, a guest, a child, a beggar, and eighthly, a goldsmith — none of these eight understand another's suffering; they think only of themselves.)

A king, a woman, Yama, a ghost, a guest, a child, a beggar, and, eighth, a goldsmith — these eight cannot recognize another's suffering; they are purely self-interested.

Kritya, then, is nothing but the disposition, born of the hatred within a person, to take some wrongful step and trouble another — and so, upon the very one who creates a kritya, the kritya itself strikes back. Whoever wishes ill upon another is the first to suffer ill himself.

An episode. The tale of the father, Dadhichi, and the son, Pippalad, and their devotion to Shiva.

There was, of that same Dadhichi, a devoted son named Pippalad. His father, the sage Dadhichi, in order to destroy the demon Vritrasura, had donated his own body, while still living, to the gods; from his bones Indra fashioned the thunderbolt (vajra) and destroyed Vritrasura. The gods then lived on happily. But on this side, the sage Dadhichi's own hermitage, without its sage, fell utterly desolate — plagued by demons, without proper food or shelter, its administration collapsed entirely after the passing of its sage-guru.

His son Pippalad thought to himself: "So this is it — how selfish the gods are! When they had need of him, Indra and all the other gods used to come [to my father]. Now, not one of them even inquires after us. Since my father's passing, we — everyone in this hermitage — have become utterly helpless, yet the gods pay us no heed at all. These gods deserve to be taught a lesson; they need to be brought to their senses."

Pippalad then performed austerities in worship of Shiva, and Shiva appeared before him in person and said, "Ask for a boon." Pippalad asked: "O Shiva, Lord of all! Grant me a kritya-demoness, so that she may destroy all the gods."

Shiva said: "My son, your father was a great benefactor — he gave the very gift of his body to the gods without any hope of return. Where did such a perverse thought come to you from?" Pippalad replied: "What you say is true, but the gods are selfish, and they must be taught a lesson." The Lord said, "So be it," and a terrifying kritya appeared before them. Pippalad said to her: "Go to heaven and destroy the gods."

No sooner had she heard this command than the kritya, baring her fearsome mouth wide, rushed straight at Pippalad himself. Pippalad grew afraid, drew back, and began to protest: "O kritya! You are meant to go to heaven, meant to destroy the gods — why have you rushed at me first, before anyone else?"

The kritya replied: "Good sage! This very body of yours is heaven itself — the gods dwell within your body too. The gods dwelt within your father's body as well, and that is why his body was itself like heaven. I shall first destroy the gods dwelling within your own body, then those of the sages nearby, and then I shall go on to destroy the whole of heaven and all its gods."

Pippalad then remembered the eternal Lord Shiva, and Sadashiv appeared and said to him: "My son! What the kritya says is true — this very body is heaven, for if we turn our senses toward the good path, toward noble objects, that is heaven; and if we turn our senses toward base and vile objects, that is hell. Whoever becomes master of his own senses is a deva [a shining, godlike being]; whoever becomes a slave to the objects of his senses is a danava [a demon]."

At Pippalad's entreaty, Shiva withdrew the kritya. Having explained this mystery of gods and demons, Shiva then vanished from sight. Pippalad's vengeful disposition dissolved, and he took up once again the practice of vows, austerity, and the study of scripture, and thus purified and brightened his own understanding.

In connection with this episode, Kabirji composed a beautiful pada:

_janko mein aadhin sahaai._
_jab durvasa vaikunth sidhaaye. tab e katha sunaai ||teka||_
_vadat ved brahmanya dev tum. karunamay sukhdayi ||_
_jaarat hai mohe chakra sudarshan. ab moh leho chhodaai ||1||_
_je jan mothe kachhu na raakhe. mamta maan badaai ||_
_take vishay vikaar aapada. mope sahi na jaai ||2||_
_ulat jaao rishi tum nrupcharane. ve raakhego bhaai ||_
_kahat kabir jankee mahima. shripati shrimukh gaai ||3||_
(U.Dh.Pan.Ma. – page 580-5) (I am subject and helper to My devotee. When Durvasa arrived in Vaikunth, this account was then related, as the refrain: "The Vedas declare You, O God who protects the Brahmins, to be full of compassion and the bestower of joy. Your Sudarshan Chakra is now burning me — release me now from this torment." [The Lord replies:] "The devotee who holds nothing back from Me — no attachment, no pride, no vanity — for him, I cannot bear it when trouble, sensory affliction, or calamity befalls him." [And to the sage:] "Turn back, O sage, to the king's own feet — he, [My devotee], will protect you, brother." Kabir says: thus, from the Lord's own mouth, is sung the glory of His devotee.)

Parbrahma says: I am subject to My devotee. There is a verse in the Bhagavat relating to this very hymn:

_aham bhaktaparadhino hyasvatantra iva dvija ||_
_sadhubhirgrasta hridayo bhaktairbhaktajanapriyah ||25||_ ("O twice-born one, I am subject to My devotee, as though I were not independent at all; My heart is held captive by the saints, and My devotees are dear to Me.")

That is, the Lord says: O ignorant sage! Hear this — I am subject to My devotees; My devotees, however, are not subject to Me. When I say "subject," I mean that I am subject to My devotees. Yadunath Maharaj writes: "The Lord says, 'I am subject, just as a parrot kept in a cage becomes subject to captivity — so am I subject to the love of My devotee.' But that devotee whose very body is like the cage [in which I, the parrot, dwell] — that is, those human beings who are My supreme devotees — within the bodies of such devotees dwells the parrot, that is, the Supreme Being. This parrot [that is, God] resides within the cage that is the devotee's own body. And if you ask whether this is constant, then, yes, it continues without a break — for [only] then do I protect everyone; yet [in truth] I am never far from My devotee."

From the Sol Padi Parachari — "The Lord is ever subject to His devotee" — Kabirji says:

_kabir das dukhi to hari dukhi, antar ekla roop ||_
_nirgun sagun ekta, avigat roop niroop ||17||_ (Kabir says: when the devotee suffers, Hari too suffers, for at heart they are one and the same being. The nirgun and sagun are one; His form is beyond description [avigat] — truly formless.)

Meaning: Baba Kabirji says that when the devotee suffers, God suffers too, because to God, whether nirgun or sagun, it is all one and the same. The nirgun God dwells within His devotee in embodied, sagun manner, as one with him — and this is avigat, beyond description, that is, His true nature cannot be known in detail; He has no fixed, definite form whatsoever.

"My devotees are exceedingly dear to Me; for their sake I revel [and remain subject] in their company, and My very name is 'Bhaktavatsal' [tender toward devotees] — I am not tender in any other way."

That is: the Lord says that My love flows ceaselessly and without interruption toward every single soul, and I take care and protect everyone equally. But before My devotees, I am subject — and it is toward them that My love flows in special abundance. Moreover, whenever anyone commits an offense against My devotee, or causes him suffering, it becomes My very first duty to protect him. Hence I even punish the soul who offends against My devotee. It is for this very reason that My name has become "Bhaktavatsal."

The Lord says: I am tender toward My devotees; I am not tender in any other way. There is a further verse relating to this, which is:

_yavadanyashrayasyaat bhagavaanapi tam janam ||_
_vilokyenna kripaya hyananyajana vatsala ||12||_ (As long as any person takes refuge in another [deity], the Lord does not look upon him with grace — for He is tender only toward those who have no other refuge.)

For as long as anyone remains dependent upon another god, the Lord does not look upon him with grace, since He is tender only toward those who take refuge in Him alone.

The Bhagavat, Canto 9, Chapter 5, verses 18 to 21, states: Ambarish's mind ever dwelt upon the lotus feet of the Lord; his speech he kept for singing Hari's glories, his hands for service to Him. His ears he kept for hearing Hari's stories, his eyes for beholding the Lord's form — thus he kept every limb, his whole body and mind, wholly engaged in devotion to the Lord.

Yet he became entangled through the vow of Ekadashi — for Ekadashi is [as tricky as] both a moneylender and a thief; going to take refuge in it, his turn came to suffer. But because his devotion to the Lord was single-pointed and unwavering, the Lord protected him. There is a line in the pada "Mein Janko Aadhin Sadai" —

_vadat ved brahman dev tum karunamai sukhdayi ||_
_jaalat he mohe chakra sudarshan ha prabhu deho chhudaai ||18||_ (The Vedas declare You, O Brahman-deity, to be compassionate, the giver of joy. Your Sudarshan Chakra is now burning me — O Lord, please release me from it!)

In this verse it is said: O Parbrahma, the Vedas declare You to be compassionate, the giver of joy — so this Sudarshan is now burning me; O Lord, release me from this. (Yet there remains an explanation to be given, as to why the Lord did not release Durvasa.) Regarding the doubt raised by this line, Revered Yadunath Maharaj has noted the following:

"A doubt has arisen: is it not the Lord's own vow that whatever sinner comes to Him for refuge, He grants him freedom from fear? Now Durvasa, too, went for refuge, yet was not protected — but the Lord's own word is: 'I forgive every sin, but two sins I do not forgive: one, an offense against My devotees, and the other, an offense against My own Name.'"

_pahunche vaikunth jaay kahyo dukh akulaay ||_
_haay haay raakhau prabhu, kharau tan jaarai hai ||1||_
_main to hau aadhin, teen gun ko na maan mere ||_
_bhakt vatsalyagun sab hi ko taare hai ||1||_ (Reaching Vaikunth, [Durvasa] cried out in anguish, "Alas, alas — save me, Lord, my body is truly burning!" [The Lord replied:] "I am indeed subject [to My devotee]; I give no heed to My own three [great] qualities — My quality of tenderness toward My devotee overrides them all.")

1) You are the protector of those who seek refuge, and I have taken refuge in You.
2) You are the destroyer of the afflicted's suffering, and I am afflicted.
3) You are the Brahmanya-deva [the god who protects Brahmins], and I am a Brahmin.

Hearing this, the Lord said: "What you say is true, but I am subject to My devotees; at this moment I give no thought to the qualities [you have named] above, for My quality of tenderness toward My devotee now takes precedence over all three of these."

While the Lord was speaking thus, Durvasa was listening — and He continued: "O Great One! Go there now [to the king]." The distressed Durvasa then went to Ambarish. The verse for this occasion:

_evam bhagavatadishto durvasashchakratapitah ||_
_ambarishamupavritya tatpadau dukhitograhit ||26||_ (Thus commanded by the Lord, and tormented by the Chakra, the sorrowful Durvasa went to Ambarish and clasped his feet.)

Thus commanded by the Lord, and tormented by the Sudarshan Chakra, the sorrowful Durvasa came to Ambarish and clasped his feet.

Vasudev [the Lord] said to Durvasa: "O sage, as long as one's [prior] karma remains attached, that karma cannot be shed — its effect must run its course." Hearing this word from the Lord, [Durvasa], together with all the gods — the all-compassionate Maharudra, Brahma, Narada, and the rest — came to Ambarish in Ayodhya. Seeing Ambarish from a distance, Durvasa prostrated himself full length upon the ground and clasped his feet — yet even so, the flame of the Sudarshan Chakra did not subside. Then the all-compassionate Lord Himself spoke: "O King! The sage has bowed at your feet — now call off the Chakra." Ambarish then spoke as follows: "O Great One! Who am I [that I should command it — where am I, and where are You]? All this manifold glory belongs to You alone. Moreover, I am pure in my own mind — where would a person of such dull understanding as I find such great power? Let me, further, explain with a clear example: when Durvasa came to our temple, we joyfully sang the praises of Govindji's qualities; and even when Durvasa pronounced his curse upon me, I did not suffer the least distress. This entire episode has been enacted by none other than the all-compassionate Lord Himself, out of grace and compassion, in order to magnify the glory of His own devotee — what part have I played in it at all? Durvasa has bowed at the king's feet in the presence of all the assembled gods, and everyone's joy knows no bounds. So, O Sudarshan and all — if my mind has been pure from beginning to end and in between, then withdraw from the sage's body."

Hearing the king speak these words, the flames of the Sudarshan Chakra subsided. Everyone was struck with wonder. Durvasa was overjoyed as the flames died away. The narrator of the Bhagavat, Shukadevji, describes it thus:

_aho anantadasanam mahatvam drishtamadya me ||_
_kritagasoapi yad rajan mangalani sameehase ||13||_
9-5-14 (Ah! Today I have witnessed the greatness of the Endless One's loving devotees. O King, though I have wronged you, still you wish only well for me.)

"Ah! Today I have witnessed the greatness of the Lord's beloved devotees. O King, I committed an offense against you, and yet you sought only my well-being."

_yannamashrutimatrena puman bhavati nirmalah ||_
_tasya tirthapadah kim va dasanamavashishyate ||14||_
9-5-16 (For those souls who become pure through the mere hearing of His auspicious Name, what task remains left for the servants of that Lord whose very feet are like a place of pilgrimage?)

"For a soul that becomes pure simply through the hearing of His auspicious Name, what task can possibly remain for His devotees — those for whom His very feet are as sacred as a place of pilgrimage?"

The Bhagavat, Canto 9, Chapter 5, verses 19 to 25, relates: King Ambarish, having performed every act of hospitality and service, still had not eaten his own meal, in the hope that the sage might yet return. And indeed the sage did return; the king served him a fine meal, the sage was pleased, and he then departed for Brahmalok.

In this way, a full year passed before the sage returned. The king, meanwhile, waited to see the sage, sustaining himself only on sips of water throughout that time; only after feeding the returned sage did the king himself take food. There is an important verse of the Bhagavat concerning this:

_evam vidhanekagunah sa raja paratmani brahmani vasudeve ||_
_kriyakalapaih samuvaha bhaktim yayaavirichyan nirayanshchakara ||25||_
9.5-25 (Thus that king, endowed with such manifold virtues, offered his devotion through the totality of his actions to Vasudev, the Supreme Being, the Brahma — and through that devotion he came to regard even the pleasures up to and including Brahmalok as no better than hell.)

That king — once Durvasa had eaten and departed — himself then took food, and Ambarish held the firm conviction that this whole episode had come to pass entirely through the Lord's own power. Holding to this conviction, he devoted himself to the Lord's worship, and through that devotion, he came to regard all pleasures — even up to those of Brahmalok — as little better than hell.

(To the west of Mathura, beyond the Saraswati temple, on the way from the Chamunda temple toward Mathura, one comes upon Ambarish Tila [Ambarish Hillock], where King Ambarish is said to have performed austerities. There, at the base of the hillock today stands the math [monastery] of Jaharpir, and atop the hillock stands a temple of Hanuman. Narada is said to have sent Dhruva to perform austerities at this very spot, because the Lord remains ever near and present there.

The hermitage of Durvasa was situated on a hill of that name, one mile from the town of Kahalgaon (Colgony) in the district of Bhagalpur; or, alternatively, this hermitage is placed six miles south-east of Rajauli, in the Nawada taluka of Gaya district.)

Revered Yadunath [Maharaj], in his account-notes, page 50, records a pada by Agradas:

_ham bhaktanson bhooli bigaari ||_
_janyon nahi ito bal inko ye harike adhikaari ||_
_kamal paraag bhanvar bhal jaanai vahe basana bihaari ||_
_nipat naalke nikat meduka bhayo keechako chaari ||_
_kaam krodh mad atishay jadmati tap bal badhyo vikaari ||_
_angeekaar kiye hari inko yah kachhu ham na bichaari ||_
_durvasa ambarish aage kari dinta bhaari ||_
_agradas abhimaan potari rishi shirte tab daari ||_ (I, unknowingly, wronged one of His devotees — I did not know that so much strength lay in him, for these are the rightful ones of Hari. The bee well knows the pollen of the lotus and delights, playfully, in its fragrance — yet the frog, though right beside the lotus stalk, remains stuck in the mud instead. Through my own foolish understanding, and the pride swollen by the strength of my austerities, my faults — lust, anger, arrogance — grew all the greater. The Lord had already accepted him [Ambarish] as His own, and this I never once considered. Durvasa, before Ambarish, showed the deepest humility, and Agradas [says]: the burden of his pride he then cast down from his own head.)

"Durvasaji wandered for a full year, but the king, exactly as before, filled with compassion, remained standing fixed in one place."

In the book Harmala of the Jaipur Parthara [tradition], on page 96, it is recorded that Maharaj Shyamdasji of the Agalod (Sardarpur) gadi [seat] composed seven padas, in the Kedara raga, called the "Ambarish-Durvasa Saptapadi" (the seven verses of Ambarish and Durvasa).

_surpati sabha bani neeki._

_kaha bhao maarag kyene rokyo. nar narendra nahi aave ||_
_brahmalok shivlok sarag sab. reete bhare na aave ||su||2||_
_kar jori doot yun bolat. sabha sabe chit dije ||_

_sab mili kahet kou hai aiso. vrat khandit jo karyahi ||_

_kahat shyam boho vidhi stuti kar. dhaay charan lapataane ||su||6||_ (Indra's assembly was beautifully arrayed. There Shiva, Brahma, Indra, and all the goddesses of power were discussing one single matter: What had happened? Who had blocked the path? — for no human soul, whether commoner or king, was arriving there any more; Brahmalok, Shivlok, and all of heaven remained empty, with none coming to fill them. Then the messenger [of Yama], hands folded, spoke thus: "Let the whole assembly listen closely: Ambarish keeps the Lord's vow with firm resolve — so what shall we resolve to do?" All together said: "Is there anyone who can cause that vow to be broken? Whatever he asks, we shall all together grant it — even should he ask for something crude and uncivilized, we shall still grant it." Hearing this, Durvasa spoke up: "I shall break his vow. In my wrath I shall hold back all three worlds — even should he prove imperishable, I shall yet burn him." Having made this vow, he arrived at dawn; then Ambarish rejoiced. Shyamdasji says: [Ambarish] praised him in many ways, and ran to clasp his feet.)

Indra's court was beautifully assembled; there Shiva, Brahma, Indra, and all the goddesses of power were discussing this one matter — how had this come to be, and who had blocked the way, that no human souls were coming there any longer: Brahmalok, Shivlok, and all of heaven remained empty, with none arriving to fill them. Then the servant — the messenger of Yama — folded his hands and began to speak: "Let all assembled here listen with attention: Ambarish keeps the Lord's vow with firm resolve — so what shall we resolve to do, what shall we consider?" All together they said: "Is there anyone who can break this vow? Whatever he then asks, we shall all together grant — even should he ask for something crude and savage, we shall still grant it." Hearing this, Durvasa said he would break his vow: "In my wrath, I shall hold back all three worlds. If he be imperishable, then—
